blocks.text: 前沿 AI 系统有潜力通过智能地探索庞大的组合搜索空间（例如，一个仅含 100 个氨基酸的蛋白质就至少对应 20100 种可能的序列）来变革生物学研究和药物发现，这要求进行动态的多候选探索。我们的长期研究愿景是，AI 智能体不仅能提出构想和分析，还能运行实验室实验来检验其假设、从结果中学习并自我改进以解决复杂问题——这一切都由人类的科学能动性驱动。

blocks.text: 实现这一愿景需要解决两个相互交织的挑战：第一，前沿模型仍无法可靠地对三维几何和物理状态进行推理——这给专用液体处理机器人的自动化带来了问题，这些机器人负责在湿实验室中移动试剂、追踪体积并执行分子生物学方案。第二，尽管智能体的假设生成和 in-silico 设计正在迅速发展，需要反复进行真实世界反馈循环来验证提案并探索庞大的搜索空间，但真实世界的湿实验室实验却未能跟上步伐，使得实验读数比以往任何时候都更像是瓶颈。

blocks.text: 让智能体扎根于物理现实

inlines.text: 让智能体扎根于物理现实

blocks.text: 首先，我们提出 VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories（VERID）框架，以弥合 AI 智能体的高层推理与湿实验室复杂且易出错的物理现实之间的差距。它是实验室工作单元的语义数字孪生，即一个实时、有状态的 3D 体积实体树，追踪从机械臂几何结构到单个孔板体积、试剂身份和移液器吸头库存的一切。

blocks.text: VERID 构建在开源 PyLabRobot framework 之上，提供四项核心能力：

inlines.text: VERID 构建在开源
PyLabRobot framework
之上，提供四项核心能力：
实时 3D 状态追踪：
允许智能体在行动前检查工作台布局、孔板体积和可用吸头。
快速虚拟空运行：
在数秒内模拟方案，以便在接触试剂前发现碰撞或空孔。
硬件安全检查：
在无效命令到达机器人之前将其拦截。
同步视频与操作日志：
捕获每次运行的完整记录，以确保研究严谨性、可复现性和调试能力。

blocks.text: 在我们的报告中，我们通过案例研究展示了这些能力的实际应用。首先，同步的视频和执行轨迹捕捉到了因分液过于靠近孔板底部而导致的不均匀染料分层，使智能体得以改进其混合策略。在同一轮实验中，持续存在的数字孪生状态使智能体能够在运行中途从读板机故障中恢复，而无需重新移液。其次，当模拟器拒绝了一个在物理上无法放入狭窄槽中的8通道吸液操作时，智能体即时重新规划，并设计了一项有针对性的析因诊断，分离出由吸头壁残留携带造成的细微偏差，而仅靠重复实验本会遗漏这一问题。最后，在一项闭环自我对弈实验中，一个智能体迭代地设计和运行机器人实验，从俯视相机图像中重建盲法染料混合物，并在多次运行中识别出自身的光学和流体伪影，将准确率提高了五倍以上。

blocks.text: 学会用适配体学习

inlines.text: 学会用适配体学习

blocks.text: 智能体需要真实的实验读数来改进其假设，因为计算模型无法捕捉湿实验室反应中发生的全貌，也无法取代实证验证。在“适配体作为实验室在环智能体分子发现的沙盒”中，我们使用结合蛋白质的DNA适配体，在3个设计-测试-迭代周期内与AI智能体一起对闭环实验室进行原型验证。适配体发现是临床生物标志物发现研究中常见的一类实验。一个完整的适配体设计-测试-分析周期仅需7–10天，因为DNA可以在混合文库中化学合成，并通过测序直接读出。在每一轮中，智能体设计候选序列，这些序列在磁珠上针对目标蛋白质进行筛选以分离功能性结合物，然后进行测序，为下一周期返回丰富的定量数据。

blocks.text: 在两个难度不同的蛋白质靶标（肌红蛋白和α-凝血酶）上进行的三个轮次中，AI驱动的理性设计和从头设计提高了经确认的靶向命中率，如下图所示（肌红蛋白和α-凝血酶分别达到33.5%和42.1%），不过每个靶标都需要识别并克服一种不同的湿实验室失败模式。

blocks.text: 在肌红蛋白上，由于智能体在第2轮中优先考虑原始结合亲和力，它们大量富集了G-四链体基序（占设计的63%）。虽然原始 pull-down 信号增加了，但湿实验数据显示，这些G-四链体大多是非特异性的"粘性"结合物，会附着在脱靶蛋白和裸磁珠上，导致靶标特异性（从75.0%降至19.1%）和真实的、经磁珠校正的命中率（从10.2%降至3.7%）双双骤降。智能体从第2轮读数中识别出这一假象后，自主修订了第3轮的设计规则，限制混杂基序、扣除磁珠结合物，并转向非G4结构支架，从而恢复了特异性（72.4%），并使在靶命中率激增九倍（33.5%）。

blocks.text: 安全

inlines.text: 安全

blocks.text: 根据Google的前沿安全框架以及我们在生物韧性方面的方针，我们在工作流程的计算和湿实验两侧都构建了保障措施：

inlines.text: 根据Google的
前沿安全框架
以及我们在
生物韧性
方面的方针，我们在工作流程的计算和湿实验两侧都构建了保障措施：
安全测试平台与筛查：
我们特意选择了受控良好、无感染性且无功能增益风险的生物系统作为测试平台，以评估智能体行为并及早发现偏差。每一个设计的序列都要经过生物安全筛查。
执行前模拟：
通过 VERID，智能体绝不会将未经核实的代码直接发送给液体处理机器人。每个实验方案都会在模拟中进行干运行，并在接触试剂前对照数字孪生进行验证。
人类监督：
由人类直接授权和审查设计的序列，验证湿实验室实验方案，并监督机器人运行。

blocks.text: 随着 AI 智能体承担更多设计-测试循环的工作，新的安全性和可靠性挑战也随之出现。迈向自主湿实验室需要解决这些开放性问题，同时为人类能动性和监督提供机会：确保智能体针对真实靶标结合进行优化，而非意外的实验捷径；验证多步骤湿实验室实验方案；并持续监控智能体的推理和执行轨迹。

blocks.text: Frontier AI systems have the potential to transform biology research and drug discovery by intelligently navigating vast combinatorial search spaces (e.g., a single 100-amino-acid protein spans at least 20100 possible sequences) calling for dynamic multi-candidate exploration. Our long-term research vision is that AI agents will not only ideate and analyze, but also run lab experiments to test their hypotheses, learn from the results, and self-improve to solve complex problems — all driven by human scientific agency.

inlines.text: Frontier AI systems have the potential to transform biology research and drug discovery by intelligently navigating vast combinatorial search spaces (e.g., a single 100-amino-acid protein spans at least 20100 possible sequences) calling for dynamic multi-candidate exploration. Our long-term research vision is that AI agents will not only ideate and analyze, but also run lab experiments to test their hypotheses, learn from the results, and self-improve to solve complex problems — all driven by human scientific agency.

blocks.text: Realizing this vision requires solving two intertwined challenges: First, frontier models still do not reason reliably about 3-dimensional geometry and physical state — which poses a problem in the automation of the specialized liquid-handling robots that move reagents, track volumes, and execute molecular biology protocols in a wet lab. Second, while agentic hypothesis generation and in-silico design are advancing rapidly, needing repeated cycles of real-world feedback to validate the proposals and navigate vast search spaces, real-world wet-lab experiments have not kept pace, making experimental readouts more of a bottleneck than ever.

Enabling AI agents to perform safe, resource efficient experimentation grounded in physical measurements by using the VERID framework.

blocks.text: Grounding agents in physical reality

inlines.text: Grounding agents in physical reality

blocks.text: First, we present the VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories (VERID) framework to bridge the gap between the high-level reasoning of AI agents and the complex, error-prone physical reality of a wet lab. It is a semantic digital twin of the laboratory workcell, i.e., a live, stateful 3D volumetric entity tree that tracks everything from robotic arm geometry to individual well volumes, reagent identities, and pipette tip inventory.

inlines.text: First, we present the
VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories

(VERID) framework to bridge the gap between the high-level reasoning of AI agents and the complex, error-prone physical reality of a wet lab. It is a semantic digital twin of the laboratory workcell, i.e., a live, stateful 3D volumetric entity tree that tracks everything from robotic arm geometry to individual well volumes, reagent identities, and pipette tip inventory.

blocks.text: The safety of a command depends on the live physical context as well as the code. An agent can generate syntactically valid code that is physically impossible (e.g., lowering an 8-channel pipette into a narrow trough that is too short), logistically invalid (e.g., aspirating from a depleted well), or scientifically compromised by unmodeled fluidic effects.

blocks.text: Built on top of the open-source PyLabRobot framework, VERID provides four core capabilities:

inlines.text: Built on top of the open-source
PyLabRobot framework
, VERID provides four core capabilities:
Live 3D state tracking:
Allow agents to check deck layout, well volumes, and available tips before acting.
Fast virtual dry runs:
Simulate protocols in seconds to catch collisions or empty wells before touching reagents.
Hardware safety checks:
Block invalid commands before they reach the robot.
Synchronized video and action logs:
Capture a complete record of every run for research rigor, reproducibility, and debugging.

blocks.text: In our report, we show these capabilities in action through case studies. First, synchronized video and execution traces caught uneven dye stratification caused by dispensing too close to the well floor, allowing the agent to refine its mixing strategy. In the same campaign, the persistent digital twin state allowed the agent to recover mid-run from a plate-reader failure without re-pipetting. Second, when the simulator rejected an 8-channel aspiration that physically wouldn't fit in a narrow trough, the agent replanned on the fly and designed a targeted factorial diagnostic isolating a subtle bias caused by residual tip-wall carryover that replication alone would have missed. Finally, in a closed-loop self-play campaign, an agent iteratively designed and ran robot experiments to reconstruct blinded dye mixtures from overhead camera images, identifying its own optical and fluidic artifacts across runs to improve accuracy more than fivefold.

blocks.text: Learning to learn with aptamers

inlines.text: Learning to learn with aptamers

blocks.text: Agents need real experimental readouts to refine their hypotheses as computational models do not capture the full picture of what happens in a wet-lab reaction and cannot replace empirical validation. In “Aptamers as a sandbox for lab-in-the-loop agentic molecular discovery”, we use protein-binding DNA aptamers to prototype the lab in a closed loop with AI agents over 3 design-test-iteration cycles. Aptamer discovery is a type of experiment common in research efforts for clinical biomarker discovery. A complete aptamer design-test-analyze cycle takes just 7–10 days, as DNA can be chemically synthesized in pooled libraries and read out directly by sequencing. In each round, agents design candidate sequences, which are screened against target proteins on magnetic beads to isolate functional binders, and then sequenced to return rich quantitative data for the next cycle.

blocks.text: On α-thrombin, Round 1 yielded 0% binders because fixed primer overhangs disrupted folding in 48% of sequences; once the agents introduced clamped flanking stems in Round 2 and diversified in Round 3, hit rates climbed to 26.0% and then 42.1% at 98.5% specificity.

inlines.text: On α-thrombin, Round 1 yielded 0% binders because fixed primer overhangs disrupted folding in 48% of sequences; once the agents introduced clamped flanking stems in Round 2 and diversified in Round 3, hit rates climbed to 26.0% and then 42.1% at 98.5% specificity.

blocks.text: On myoglobin, as agents prioritized raw binding affinity in Round 2, they heavily enriched G-quadruplex motifs (63% of designs). While raw pull-down increased, the wet-lab data showed that most of these G-quadruplexes were non-specific "sticky" binders adhering to off-target proteins and bare magnetic beads, causing both target specificity (from 75.0% to 19.1%) and true, bead-corrected hit rate (from 10.2% to 3.7%) to plunge. Recognizing this artifact from the Round 2 readout, the agents autonomously revised their design rules for Round 3, capping promiscuous motifs, subtracting bead binders, and pivoting to non-G4 structural scaffolds to recover specificity (72.4%) and surge ninefold in on-target hit rate (33.5%).

blocks.text: Accelerating de novo protein binder design

inlines.text: Accelerating de novo protein binder design

blocks.text: Closing the loop for proteins is more complex. Unlike aptamers, which are chemically synthesized, proteins must be expressed biologically, so each loop adds cellular or cell-free selection, expression, and folding steps. Together with a larger sequence space, this creates bottlenecks on both the computational and wet-lab sides.

inlines.text: Closing the loop for proteins is more complex. Unlike aptamers, which are chemically synthesized, proteins must be expressed biologically, so each loop adds cellular or cell-free selection, expression, and folding steps. Together with a larger sequence space, this creates bottlenecks on both the computational and wet-lab sides.

blocks.text: In “Agent-guided epitope excision enables economical de novo binder design”, we applied our workflow to fibroblast activation protein alpha (FAP), a large, challenging receptor overexpressed in solid tumors. In just a few experimental runs, the top designs yielded binders with single-digit nanomolar affinity, a level of tight, drug-like binding typically achieved only after extensive rounds of laboratory optimization.

inlines.text: In “
Agent-guided epitope excision enables economical de novo binder design
”, we applied our workflow to
fibroblast activation protein alpha (FAP)

, a large, challenging receptor overexpressed in solid tumors. In just a few experimental runs, the top designs yielded binders with single-digit nanomolar affinity, a level of tight, drug-like binding typically achieved only after extensive rounds of laboratory optimization.

blocks.text: Computationally, de novo binder design requires generating candidate backbones, designing sequences to fit them, and re-folding the resulting complexes to predict binding. That final re-folding step consumes the vast majority of GPU compute, as it scales quadratically with target length. By surgically excising just the local binding pocket during folding, our pipeline accelerated each cycle more than eightfold without losing structural accuracy. This turns decisions about where to bind and how much surrounding structure to include into tactical levers that LLM agents are well-suited to optimize.

blocks.text: In a head-to-head comparison at equal compute, human–agent collaboration, where a scientist sets the high-level strategy and an agent drives tactical execution, nearly doubled the in-silico hit rate of a scientist working alone while uncovering hits across a much broader range of target sites. To scale wet-lab screening alongside our computational pipeline, we operationalized yeast surface display with fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), a workflow that allows us to screen large libraries of engineered protein variants in parallel by fluorescence.

blocks.text: Safety

inlines.text: Safety

blocks.text: In line with Google’s Frontier Safety Framework and our approach to bioresilience, we build safeguards across both the computational and wet-lab sides of our workflows:

inlines.text: In line with Google’s
Frontier Safety Framework
and our approach to
bioresilience
, we build safeguards across both the computational and wet-lab sides of our workflows:
Safe testbeds and screening:

We deliberately selected well-controlled, non-infectious biological systems without gain-of-function risk, as testbeds to evaluate agent behavior and catch drift early. Every designed sequence goes through biosecurity screening.
Simulation before execution:
Through VERID, agents never send unverified code directly to the liquid handling robots. Every protocol is dry-run in simulation and validated against the digital twin before touching reagents.
Human oversight:
Humans directly authorize and review designed sequences, verify wet-lab protocols, and supervise robot runs.

blocks.text: As AI agents take on more of the design-test cycle, new safety and reliability challenges emerge. Moving toward an autonomous wet lab requires solving these open problems with opportunities for human agency and oversight: ensuring agents optimize for true target binding rather than unintended experimental shortcuts, verifying multi-step wet-lab protocols, and continuously monitoring agent reasoning and execution traces.

blocks.text: From grounding agents in physical lab robotics, to running fast closed-loop aptamer cycles where agents learn to explore sequence space, to discovering single-digit nanomolar protein binders, these efforts form the building blocks for human-directed autonomous discovery in the life sciences. We're excited by this progress and look forward to sharing what comes next.
